corrections_established: The evaluation panel's final conclusion is dated 25 February 1982 and was approved by the Director of DCA the following day (printed p. 9). The DSB recommendation followed it on 8 March. The decision order was not previously recorded.
The DCA evaluation's recorded conclusion statement is 'REPLICA Approach Provides the Best (SIC) DoD Data Network' (printed p. 9, chart). '(SIC)' is printed in the report.

Quotation corrected: 'The use of two design teams to PREPARE WHAT WERE essentially proposals served to force a binary decision in the evaluation', printed p. 7, not 'to produce essentially proposals' at pp. 7-8.

Locator corrected: the 'well established criteria' and 'complex quantitative method based on disaggregated subjective judgments' wording is the chart on printed p. 7; the prose form, 'a complex quantitative method which relied in the end on highly disaggregated judgments', is on printed p. 9. Not pp. 7-8.

The chart on printed p. 12 lists six design-and-technology considerations: maturity, state of the art, evolutionary potential, security approach, manpower, and interconnection. The same page lists survivability, security, cost, user satisfaction, and common-user network development separately. The chart is not the full selection framework.

Locator corrected: 'the most expeditious approach is probably to accept NSA's recommendation' is on printed p. 20 alone, and continues 'for improving the security architecture of whichever system is chosen'. Not pp. 19-20.

Locator corrected: the Soviet-inventory sentence is on printed p. 16 and the 'ill-defined but seem to favor WIN/ARPANET' bullet on printed p. 15; both stand, but the extensive host-interface development passage is on printed p. 15 only, not 'pp. 11, 15'.

Misreading corrected: 'No really convincing set of comparative costs' (printed p. 23) concerns comparative costs FOR COMMON USER NETWORKS AND DEDICATED LINKS, not a comparison between REPLICA and AUTODIN II. It cannot support a claim that no comparative cost set existed for the two designs.

Incompleteness corrected: printed p. 21 records that total estimated design team costs 'were then adjusted and normalized for comparison by the evaluation team' and that 'These cost estimates gave a heavy edge to REPLICA.' A normalized comparative cost analysis therefore existed; what the Task Force doubted was its validity in absolute terms.

Printed p. 17 attributes the comparative survivability results to DCA, and pp. 17-18 reproduce two drawdown curves. The attribution and general method are documented; inputs and model runs needed to reproduce these exact curves remain unheld.
Epilogue legibility corrected: printed pp. 28-31 are legible in this text layer and were read in full. The earlier report of a degraded, fragment-only section does not hold for this copy.

Membership affiliations differ between the body list (printed p. 6) and Appendix B (printed p. 35): System Planning Corporation / Systems Planning Corporation; UCLA / University of California; HRA, Inc. / Rosenbaum Associates, Inc. Preserved, not reconciled. Van Doubleday is Major General, USAF (Ret.); Ralph E. Chatham is LCDR, USN, DSB Secretariat Representative.

Date resolved visually at printed p. 3 / PDF p. 11: 'In July 1980, an OSD review group was established'. The raw OCR's '1960' is an extraction error; the scan itself is clear. This program-wide review is a lead, not yet an explanation of the TCP upgrade deferral.

Printed pp. 6, 9, 27, 33 and 37 distinguish concurrent Task Force review from the February 25 DCA panel conclusion, February 26 Director approval, March Task Force recommendations, and the April 2 departmental order signed by Frank C. Carlucci. Neither advisory body alone issued the final cancellation order.
newly_recorded: Printed p. 1: 'The Task Force's final preference for the evolutionary ARPA Network approach was in agreement with DCA's conclusion that it was the better of the two, and was reached without regard to AUTODIN II programmatic deficiencies.'
Printed p. 12: 'It found these advantages to be more substantial than the DCA evaluation suggested that they were.'

Printed p. 12, John Stenbit's recorded note: the Task Force Evaluation 'tends to focus on considerations it felt supported the choice of the ARPANET approach, and consequently masks a substantially less obvious choice between the two systems', and 'has greater utility as guidance to proceeding with the implementation of an ARPANET decision than in providing the basis for making such a decision.' The note also explicitly says he does not take issue with the choice made; it qualifies the presentation rather than opposing the selected approach.
Printed p. 13: 'the routing algorithm used in the ARPANET system is substantially stronger than that developed for AUTODIN II', and the REPLICA topology 'substantially more sophisticated'.
Printed p. 13: 'This situation occurred in the DCA redesign of AUTODIN II for the evaluation when the number of precedence levels could not be increased because of kernel limitations.'

Printed p. 14, Interconnection Issues: incremental growth 'more compatible with the ARPANET design'; 'there is a standing set of networks already existing which can be pulled together to form ultimately a true common user network operating at all security levels'.

Printed p. 20: 'Interoperability, costs and program timing were all affected by the concerns that NSA had'; and 150,000 lines of source code in the AUTODIN II kernel-based switch against 15,000 lines of object code in the ARPANET switch. These counts use different units and do not establish a tenfold software-size ratio.

Printed p. 23: advantages of a common user network listed as 'interoperability, survivability, peakload capacity, reliability, costs'; the recommended approach is 'discrete nets of users ... maintaining a compatibility between nets that would allow for their future consolidation. This is a bottom-up rather than a top-down approach.'
Printed p. 24: the IPLI 'provides end-to-end encryption for the data carried on the network and serves as a gateway between nets.'

Printed p. 25: 'The WIN/ARPANET approach provides for three levels of host interfacing', the most desirable being to modify host software; other approaches 'tend to become expensive in terms of true interoperability'.

Printed p. 6: Task Force established late September 1981, members approved by December; met 21-22 January, 18-19 February and 4-5 March 1982, the schedule 'tied to the DCA comparative evaluation timelines'; entire DSB briefed 5 May 1982 and raised no objection.
Printed p. 27: 'The following recommendations were made to USDR&E on March 12, 1982.'

Printed p. 29: the DDN Program Office's favoured security architecture 'Option 2.2' is separate classified and unclassified networks 'connected ultimately through switch-level gates allowing classified traffic to exploit routing through the unclassified network but denying unclassified users access to the classified network'; Task Force review 6-7 October 1982; NSA questions about connecting MINET in Europe with MILNET in the U.S.
Printed p. 28: access control for dialing subscribers 'was not provided for in the REPLICA Program Plan'.

Printed pp. 18 and 20: secure operation was possible for either design, and the Task Force judged both adequately protected with NSA-proposed modifications. Its ARPANET preference did not establish that AUTODIN II security was impossible.

corrections_established: The executive summary (printed iii / PDF p. 6) limits the account to the design process through January 1982 and explicitly warns of significant process changes before publication. Its description of inadequate criteria cannot establish the criteria used at the February 25 panel conclusion.

Status qualifier, foreword: DCEC Technical Notes 'do not represent an approved position or policy of DCEC, and should not be used as authoritative guidance for related planning and/or further action.'

Locator corrected: 'far from the usable collection of clean user requirements' is on printed p. 7, and the unusable line speeds, invalid or misspelled location names and suspect mode fields are also on printed p. 7. Only 'An ADP system as described in the URDB might not correspond with the real system' is on printed p. 2. Not 'pp. 2-3'.
Locator corrected: the reconstructed baseline of 91 ADP systems, 488 host computers, 87 remote concentrators and 1359 terminals is on printed p. 8, not pp. 7-8.

Locator corrected: the single agreed criterion, the 99% gap, and 'No meaningful conclusions can be drawn from the delay calculations for the average size packets of each network' are all on printed p. 26, not pp. 25-26.
Locator refined: GUPTA printed p. 17, CULINES p. 18, MUXLOC/CONLOC p. 19, GRINDER pp. 19-21. GRINDER's ARPANET validation and the ATT 260-series and DDS rate-step tables are on printed p. 21.

'The drawdown curves ... are not in this document' is wrong as stated. Figure 2, printed p. 28, is a drawdown curve, but it is labelled a SAMPLE. The accurate statement is the report's own, printed p. 30: 'Specific results from the models are not presented herein.'

Survivability was comparatively modelled: 'Comparison of the survivability of the two network backbones was another goal of the evaluation process' (printed p. 27), and the 6-mile-radius nuclear variant was adopted to 'produce drawdown curves for each of the two designed backbones that could more meaningfully be compared' (printed p. 29).
newly_recorded: Printed p. 12: the traffic model's overhead specifications 'included consideration of segment overhead and packet overhead, both Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) overhead in the forward flow direction, and TCP acknowledgements (ACKS) in the reverse data flow direction. The practice of piggybacking TCP ACKS when possible was taken into account.' Results in Table III, REPLICA Network Overhead, printed p. 13, and Table IV, AUTODIN II Overhead, printed p. 14. The DD-1473 key words include 'TCP/IP'; the acronym list, printed p. 31, expands TCP.

Printed p. 26: the incommensurability that defeated the delay comparison is stated numerically. 'The average packet size in one network was 996 bits, in the other 4499 bits ... so a direct comparison of "average" packet delays provides no immediate insight.'

Printed p. 25, section 4 heading: 'LACK OF PERFORMANCE CRITERIA'. Printed p. 25 also records that both backbones were cost and performance verified by DCEC, with delays computed per packet and tandem loads checked against proposed switch counts.

Printed p. 30 conclusions name four problems: URDB data accuracy and consistency; design tools needing modification when applied to a different system; the need for caution and agreement so that 'neither design be affected more than the other'; and performance criteria never specified sufficiently.
Executive summary: 'The network design process was hampered by attempting to rapidly apply existing design tools suitable for the AUTODIN II approach to the different Replica approach.'

Printed p. 26 / PDF p. 35: a defined 200 ms backbone constraint applied to highest-priority 600-bit packets. The author reports no agreed minimum delay for the remaining 99 percent and calls for user-to-user whole-transaction delay criteria including access and segmentation. Inadequate criteria does not mean no criteria of any kind.

Printed p. 25 / PDF p. 34: cost and performance verification means calculations with common costing and GRINDER, not measurements of two completed networks. Difficulty adapting existing AUTODIN-II-suitable tools does not prove the origin of every tool or a biased result.
unresolved_readings: The 1359-terminal baseline still differs from the Program Plan's 1446 on the same 91 systems and 488 hosts. Preserved, not reconciled.
The document carries no reference list and cites no evaluation-team report. Its only external citation is the System Performance Specification for AUTODIN II, Phase I, printed p. 26.
